what_happened: The person running Athena split a failed job into two requests by hand. The job was to get a GitHub result (CI) used in Athena's checks. It had failed twice. Planning grew to 28 items, and the writer ran into its 3000-second deadline. The two new requests are 3rze (push the candidate to a CI branch) and n9tm (use the CI result in the checks). The person also queued g47x so a writer that hits its deadline keeps its work. No job is attached to this event. It is an intervention that overrode the normal flow, and the person did the splitting and the design.
cause: Athena accepts a multi-part request as one job with no size bound at the reading or the plan. The critic let a 28-item plan stand, and nothing in Athena splits an oversized request. The writer's fixed deadline also discards all work when it fires. So the only way out is for the person running Athena to split the request, and this has happened again on the speed path.
prevention: Add a code check at planning. When a plan exceeds a set number of items, or a forecast over one producer run's deadline, the critic must reject it. Athena then splits it into dependent jobs on its own, one per separable deliverable, and queues them in order. Together with keeping a writer's partial work at its deadline (g47x), an oversized job can no longer fail twice and need a manual split.
proposed_request: Add a plan size gate to Athena's planning stage. If a plan has more than 12 items, or its forecast writer time is over 70% of the writer deadline, the critic must return needs-splitting instead of accepting it. When a plan is returned that way, Athena splits it into dependent jobs. Each job covers one separable deliverable with its own acceptance criteria, and they are queued in dependency order. Show the split in athena status. Tests: a 28-item plan is refused and split into jobs that are each under the limit, a 10-item plan passes unchanged, and the split jobs keep the original request's acceptance criteria between them.
